{{Short description|Characterization of normable spaces}}
In [[mathematics]], '''Kolmogorov's normability criterion''' is a [[theorem]] that provides a [[necessary and sufficient condition]] for a [[topological vector space]] to be {{em|[[Normable space|normable]]}}; that is, for the existence of a [[Norm (mathematics)|norm]] on the space that generates the given [[topology]].<ref>{{cite book|title=Applied Nonlinear Functional Analysis: An Introduction|first1=Nikolaos S.|last1=Papageorgiou|first2=Patrick|last2=Winkert|publisher=Walter de Gruyter|year=2018|isbn=9783110531831|at=Theorem 3.1.41 (Kolmogorov's Normability Criterion)|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=AzCGDwAAQBAJ&pg=PT264}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=Functional Analysis: Theory and Applications|series=Dover Books on Mathematics|first=R. E.|last=Edwards|publisher=Courier Corporation|year=2012|isbn=9780486145105|contribution=Section 1.10.7: Kolmagorov's Normability Criterion|pages=85–86|contribution-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fdhi90F0HvcC&pg=PA85}}</ref> The normability criterion can be seen as a result in same vein as the [[Nagata–Smirnov metrization theorem]] and [[Bing metrization theorem]], which gives a necessary and sufficient condition for a [[topological space]] to be [[metrizable space|metrizable]].  The result was proved by the Russian mathematician [[Andrey Nikolayevich Kolmogorov]] in 1934.<ref name="Berberian1974">{{cite book|last=Berberian|first=Sterling K.|title=Lectures in Functional Analysis and Operator Theory|series=Graduate Texts in Mathematics, No. 15|publisher=Springer-Verlag|location=New York-Heidelberg|year=1974|isbn=0387900802}}</ref><ref name="Kolmogorov1934">{{cite journal|last=Kolmogorov|first=A. N.|title=Zur Normierbarkeit eines allgemeinen topologischen linearen Räumes|journal=Studia Math.|volume=5|year=1934}}</ref><ref name="Tikhomirov2007">{{cite book|last=Tikhomirov|first=Vladimir M.|chapter=Geometry and approximation theory in A. N. Kolmogorov's works|title=Kolmogorov's Heritage in Mathematics|url=https://archive.org/details/kolmogorovsherit00char_702|url-access=limited|pages=[https://archive.org/details/kolmogorovsherit00char_702/page/n159 151]&ndash;176|publisher=Springer|location=Berlin|year=2007|doi=10.1007/978-3-540-36351-4_8|editor=Charpentier, Éric|editor2=Lesne, Annick|editor3=Nikolski, Nikolaï K.}} (See Section 8.1.3)</ref>

==Statement of the theorem==

{{Math theorem|name=Kolmogorov's normability criterion|math_statement=A [[topological vector space]] is normable if and only if it is a [[T1 space|T<sub>1</sub> space]] and admits a [[Bounded set (topological vector space)|bounded]] [[Convex set|convex]] [[Neighbourhood (mathematics)|neighbourhood]] of the origin.
}}

Because translation (that is, vector addition) by a constant preserves the convexity, boundedness, and [[Translation invariant topology|openness of sets]], the words "of the origin" can be replaced with "of some point" or even with "of every point".

===Definitions===

It may be helpful to first recall the following terms:
* A {{em|[[topological vector space]]}} (TVS) is a vector space <math>X</math> equipped with a topology <math>\tau</math> such that the vector space operations of scalar multiplication and vector addition are continuous.
* A topological vector space <math>(X, \tau)</math> is called {{em|[[Normable space|normable]]}} if there is a [[Norm (mathematics)|norm]] <math>\|\cdot\|: X \to \R</math> on <math>X</math> such that the open balls of the norm <math>\|\cdot\|</math> generate the given topology <math>\tau.</math>  (Note well that a given normable topological vector space might admit multiple such norms.)
* A [[topological space]] <math>X</math> is called a {{em|[[T1 space|T<sub>1</sub> space]]}} if, for every two distinct points <math>x, y \in X,</math> there is an open [[Neighbourhood (mathematics)|neighbourhood]] <math>U_x</math> of <math>x</math> that does not contain <math>y.</math>  In a topological vector space, this is equivalent to requiring that, for every <math>x \neq 0,</math> there is an open neighbourhood of the origin not containing <math>x.</math>  Note that being T<sub>1</sub> is weaker than being a [[Hausdorff space]], in which every two distinct points <math>x, y \in X</math> admit open neighbourhoods <math>U_x</math> of <math>x</math> and <math>U_y</math> of <math>y</math> with <math>U_x \cap U_y = \varnothing</math>;  since normed and normable spaces are always Hausdorff, it is a "surprise" that the theorem only requires T<sub>1</sub>.
* A subset <math>A</math> of a vector space <math>X</math> is a {{em|[[convex set]]}} if, for any two points <math>x, y \in A,</math> the line segment joining them lies wholly within <math>A,</math> that is, for all <math>0 \leq t \leq 1,</math> <math>(1 - t) x + t y \in A.</math>
* A subset <math>A</math> of a topological vector space <math>(X, \tau)</math> is a {{em|[[Bounded set (topological vector space)|bounded set]]}} if, for every open neighbourhood <math>U</math> of the origin, there exists a scalar <math>\lambda</math> so that <math>A \subseteq \lambda U.</math>  (One can think of <math>U</math> as being "small" and <math>\lambda</math> as being "big enough" to inflate <math>U</math> to cover <math>A.</math>)
